title: Simple General Partnership Agreement
summary: Two partners set out contributions, profit split, decisions and what happens if one leaves.
useWhen: Two people are running a small business together as a general partnership and want their deal in writing.
watchOuts: In a general partnership each partner is usually personally liable for all partnership debts, including debts caused by the other partner. Many businesses form an LLC instead.
Register a trade name ('doing business as') if the state or county requires it, and get an EIN. A partnership files Form 1065 and gives each partner a Schedule K-1.
Without an agreement, state partnership law (often based on the Uniform Partnership Act) supplies default rules, such as equal profit shares regardless of contributions.
Set a valuation method for buyouts now. Disagreements about value are the most common partnership fight.

sections.title: 1. Partners and name
sections.body:
**Partner A:** {{partner_a_name}}, {{partner_a_address}} ({{partner_a_email}})

**Partner B:** {{partner_b_name}}, {{partner_b_address}} ({{partner_b_email}})

The partners form a general partnership named {{business_name}} (the "Partnership"), starting on {{effective_date}}, with its principal office at {{principal_office}}.

sections.title: 3. Contributions
4. Profits, losses and pay
sections.body:
Profits and losses are shared: Partner A {{share_a}}%, Partner B {{share_b}}%.

{{draws}}

sections.title: 5. Management and decisions
6. Duties
sections.body: Each partner will devote the time and effort reasonably needed for the business, act in good faith, and not compete with the Partnership or take its business opportunities for themselves without the other partner's written consent.

sections.title: 7. Books, bank accounts and taxes
sections.body: The Partnership will keep complete books, open accounts in its own name, and file its own tax returns. Each partner may inspect the books at any time. The partners will agree on an accountant.

sections.title: 8. A partner leaving
sections.body: A partner may withdraw with 90 days' written notice. If a partner withdraws, dies or becomes permanently disabled, the other partner may continue the business and buy the departing partner's interest. The price is the value of the interest determined by {{valuation_method}} as of the departure date. The price may be paid over up to {{buyout_months}} months, with interest at the applicable federal rate. If the remaining partner does not elect to buy within 60 days, the Partnership will be wound up.

sections.title: 9. Disputes
sections.body: The partners will first try to resolve disputes by talking in good faith, then by mediation with a mutually chosen mediator, before going to court.

sections.title: 10. Dissolution
sections.body: If the Partnership dissolves, the partners will collect receivables, sell assets as needed, pay debts and then distribute what is left according to capital accounts and then profit shares.

sections.title: 11. General terms
sections.body:
- **Whole agreement.** This document (with any attachments named in it) is the parties' entire agreement on its subject and replaces earlier discussions and drafts.
- **Changes.** It can only be changed in a writing signed by all parties.
- **Severability.** If a court finds any part unenforceable, that part is limited to the minimum extent needed and the rest stays in effect.
- **No waiver.** Not enforcing a term once is not a waiver of it later.
- **Notices.** Notices must be in writing and delivered by hand, by a recognized courier, by certified mail, or by email to the addresses in this document (or a later address a party gives in writing). Email notice is effective when sent unless the sender receives a bounce-back.
- **Governing law.** The law of the state of {{governing_state}} governs this agreement, without regard to conflict-of-law rules.
- **Counterparts and electronic signatures.** This agreement may be signed in counterparts and electronically. Each party consents to doing business electronically under the federal E-SIGN Act and the state's version of the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (or New York's Electronic Signatures and Records Act). An electronic signature has the same effect as a handwritten one.
